title: Integrated wastewater and clinical genomic surveillance for high-resolution tracking of measles virus evolution and transmission
desc: Measles outbreaks have surged globally, challenging surveillance and control efforts. In South Africa, the 2024−2025 measles outbreak led to nearly 4,000 reported cases, triggering a nationwide vaccination campaign. However, tracking measles virus (MeV; species Morbillivirus hominis ) transmission and evolution remains difficult at scale, particularly in settings with limited access to care, diagnostic testing and sequencing capacity. Wastewater can enable population-scale virus surveillance, but low MeV concentrations limit detection sensitivity and sequencing quality. Here we show that overcoming these technical challenges enables integrated wastewater and clinical genomic surveillance that expands the coverage and resolution of MeV monitoring. We developed a virus concentration and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) workflow and applied it to 4,502 wastewater samples collected across all nine provinces of South Africa during the 2024−2025 outbreak. Wastewater MeV genotype prevalence tracked clinical estimates, and phylogenetic analyses combining wastewater and clinical sequences revealed geographically structured transmission and previously undetected inter-provincial spread. WGS recovered transmission links not captured by the field standard approach, which targets a 450-nucleotide region of the nucleoprotein gene (N450), highlighting the importance of WGS to accurately characterize transmission dynamics. Our study provides a cost-effective and scalable genomic surveillance approach to support measles control and elimination. Whole-genome sequencing and phylogenetic analyses of wastewater and surveillance samples during the 2024−2025 measles outbreak in South Africa reveal previously undetected inter-provincial spread and transmission links, suggesting that wastewater-integrated whole-genome surveillance can improve measles monitoring and control efforts.

title: Artificial intelligence capacity in the rural United States: a national qualitative study.
source: PubMed · Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
desc: [Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA] To understand how rural hospitals use artificial intelligence (AI) and identify ways to reduce the barriers to safe, effective use of high-quality tools that align with these hospitals' key priorities. Stratified random sample drawn from the full population of critical access hospitals (CAHs) in the United States in 2025 (n = 1377) to approximate proportional representation of the 4 census regions. We conducted in-depth qualitative interviews with hospital leadership (eg, CMIOs, CIOs, IT leads) tasked with decision-making about technology. Interviews were conducted between October 20, 2025, and January 23, 2026. Drawn from the full population of CAHs in the US in 2025, 256 hospitals were sampled and interviews were completed for a total of 50 CAHs represented by 73 interview participants. Generative AI applications were more common and seen as more valuable for CAH contexts than traditional predictive AI. Primary barriers included infrastructure limitations, cost, and lack of transparency on how AI tools worked. Despite a desire to implement robust governance, most CAHs did not have the ability to do so and reported a critical need for information, tools, and policies to build their AI governance capacity. Information (peer learning, information from non-commercial sources), tools (registries, model cards), and policy to support technical capacity were perceived as the most responsive ways to build capacity. To reduce structural barriers to safe and effective AI decision-making, resources and investment should focus on information sharing with and across rural organizations, AI governance support, and transparency efforts. This will support CAHs in judiciously leveraging available resources and prevent waste on low-quality or misaligned AI tools.

title: Machine Learning and Deep Learning for Predicting Response and Outcomes After Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of ECG-Based Models.
desc: [Medical sciences (Basel, Switzerland)] Background/Objectives: Up to 40% of patients receiving cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) do not experience significant clinical improvement, highlighting the limitations of conventional selection criteria. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied to electrocardiogram (ECG) and other clinical data to improve patient selection. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the performance and methodological quality of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models using ECG-derived information to predict CRT response and clinical outcomes. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus and Web of Science for studies published between January 2006 and April 2026. Eligible studies developed or evaluated ML or DL algorithms primarily using pre-implantation ECG data to predict CRT response, including changes in left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) or left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV), or mortality. Model performance and prognostic associations were synthesized using random-effects meta-analyses of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and hazard ratios (HRs), respectively. Methodological quality and risk of bias were assessed using the PROBAST+AI tool. Results: We identified 14 eligible studies containing 34 distinct model evaluations. Most models utilized digital 12-lead ECG waveforms or single representative beats. Across 26 model-outcome estimates, the exploratory pooled AUROC was 0.710 (95% CI: 0.660-0.759), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 94.7%; p < 0.001). Across 10 heterogeneous model-outcome estimates, the exploratory pooled HR was 1.75 (95% CI: 1.42-2.15; I2 = 83.3%), although differences in prognostic constructs and endpoints precluded interpretation as a common effect. ML models had a higher pooled AUROC than DL models (0.752 vs. 0.669; exploratory Wald test: difference = 0.084; 95% CI: 0.002-0.165; p = 0.044). Pooled HR estimates also differed (ML: 2.22; DL: 1.46; ratio = 1.51; p < 0.001). These indirect subgroup comparisons were limited by clinical and methodological heterogeneity and potential dependence among estimates. PROBAST+AI assessment identified a high overall risk of bias in 32 of the 34 models, with concerns concentrated primarily in the participants and data sources and analysis domains. title: Learning the Malignant Transformation of Lung Adenocarcinoma Cells Using Explainable AI
desc: Tumor evolution in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) drives drug resistance and disease progression, yet the cellular transitions underlying the malignant transformation of cells remain poorly understood. Comparing this progression of cancer cells across patients is challenging owing to substantial inter-patient cell heterogeneity. Here, based on single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) data of 227 patients with LUAD including 422,727 tumor cells, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of tumor cell progression and developed Global Tumor Time (GTT), a continuous measure of tumor cell progression across patients. GTT provided a scalable and biologically meaningful metric of tumor progression that aligned with clinicopathological, transcriptomic and spatial characteristics of malignancy and demonstrated robust prognostic performance (C-index = 0.60), which was further validated in two external datasets comprising snRNA-seq (C-index = 0.66) and bulk RNA sequencing (C-index = 0.61). Using explainable AI to investigate the molecular correlates of GTT, we identified two distinct transcriptional programs associated with early and late progression states. These findings establish a scalable and interpretable framework for reconstructing malignant cell transformation across patients and allow for investigating the biology of tumor progression at single-cell resolution.

Performance of intracortical microelectrode arrays in people with implanted brain–computer interfaces over a 20-year period
desc: Utah arrays recorded stable spiking activity for up to 7.3 years, with modest signal decline on average and sustained movement decoding in the majority of arrays analyzed, demonstrating the long-term feasibility of intracortical brain–computer interfaces. The silicon microelectrode ‘Utah’ array has enabled people with paralysis to control computer cursors, operate prosthetic limbs and communicate using high-performance brain–computer interfaces. However, reports so far have typically been limited to one or two individuals, with no systematic assessment of array longevity, decoding accuracy and day-to-day stability. Here we present a comprehensive 20-year evaluation of neural data from the BrainGate clinical trials, spanning 2,289 recording sessions, 20 arrays and 14 participants. On average, arrays successfully recorded neural spiking waveforms on 35.6% of electrodes, with a modest 7 percentage point decline over the recording period (up to 7.3 years). Using a ‘decoding signal-to-noise ratio’ (dSNR) metric, we found that 11 of 14 arrays provided meaningful movement decoding throughout participation (median dSNR >1), with three achieving >70% accuracy compared with able-bodied mouse control. We also found that dSNR increased approximately logarithmically with the number of electrodes, providing a pathway for scaling performance. While longevity exceeded previous nonhuman primate studies, achieving peak performance consistently may require further improvements.

title: Artificial intelligence in influenza prevention and control: translational pathways, supporting evidence, and system-level challenges.
desc: [Frontiers in public health] Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to influenza prevention and control. AI encompasses conventional machine learning, deep learning, and protein language models. Large language models (LLMs) are an emerging subset of AI. Current evidence remains weakly linked to real-world workflows and population health outcomes. This structured narrative review proposes a three-stage translational maturity framework. Phase I is technical efficacy assessment. Phase II is implementation effectiveness verification. Phase III is population impact and sustainability. We synthesized evidence in three domains: viral evolution prediction and vaccine design; epidemic surveillance and early warning; and individual-level infection risk detection and clinical monitoring. We used a three-level evidence hierarchy. Level A is influenza-specific evidence. Level B is transferable evidence from other infectious diseases. Level C is general biomedical or methodological evidence. Only two Phase II studies were identified, both in epidemic surveillance and early warning; no Phase II studies were identified in virus evolution and vaccine design or in individual-level infection risk detection. No study met the prespecified Phase III criteria. Phase III requires demonstrated downstream population health benefit. Prospective deployment or improved forecasting alone is not sufficient. Across domains, bottlenecks have shifted from model accuracy to governance, interpretability, accountability, interoperability, workflow integration, equity, and sustainable monitoring. LLMs attract major attention, but their influenza-specific evidence remains limited. Their greatest value may lie in augmenting, not replacing, specialized models and human expertise. We propose phase-specific evidence thresholds, implementation-oriented evaluation metrics, an implementation readiness checklist, and priority evidence gaps for translating AI-enabled influenza tools into implementation-ready public health applications.

title: BYSTER: multimodal graph learning resolves bystander versus tumor-specific T cell states in the tumor immune microenvironment
desc: Bystander T cells infiltrate tumors without recognizing tumor antigens and constitute a substantial component of the tumor microenvironment. Whether they are passive residents or active participants in antitumor immunity, and how they influence immunotherapy response, remains poorly understood, largely because transcriptional states and T-cell receptor (TCR) sequences alone do not reliably resolve antigen specificity. Here, we developed BYSTER, a heterogeneous graph neural network that integrates transcriptional representations with paired TCR representations through cross-modal message passing at metacell and metaTCR resolution. Across three datasets with distinct definitions of tumor specificity, BYSTER achieved mean AUROCs of 0.729 to 0.920, outperforming unimodal and conventional multimodal baselines, and ablation analyses confirmed the contribution of cross-modal message passing. Application to lung and pancreatic cancer cohorts revealed distinct biological characteristics of the two predicted populations. Bystander T cells were enriched for naive and memory subsets and MAIT-like cells expressing SLC4A10, and exhibited inflammatory and cellular stress-associated programs, including TNF signaling via NF-{kappa}B and hypoxia. Notably, these transcriptional patterns were consistent across lung and pancreatic cancers, with tumor-specific T cells showing enrichment of cell cycle and proliferation-associated programs in both cancer types. Spatial analyses further revealed distinct inferred communication patterns, with bystander T cells showing associations with inflammatory ligand-receptor interactions involving myeloid populations. Responders to immunotherapy contributed a larger proportion of the predicted bystander compartment, suggesting an association between bystander T-cell abundance and an immune-responsive microenvironment. BYSTER thus links predicted T-cell antigen specificity to transcriptional states, spatial organization and clinical response, highlighting the potential importance of bystander T cells in tumor immunity.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Detection of Tumor Calcification in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma: Emerging Opportunities in Computational Oral Pathology and Biomineralization Research.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Objective: Tumor-associated calcification is increasingly recognized as a potentially relevant feature of the tumor microenvironment across multiple malignancies; however, its significance in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains poorly understood and is frequently overlooked during routine histopathologic assessment. This perspective examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted computational pathology to improve the detection, quantification, and spatial characterization of tumor-associated calcification in OSCC and discusses its potential as an emerging histopathologic research phenotype and candidate biomarker requiring further validation. Design: A narrative synthesis of the current literature was undertaken to evaluate the biological mechanisms underlying tumor-associated calcification in OSCC, recent advances in biomineralization research, and the application of AI and computational pathology in digital histopathology. Current evidence was integrated to propose future AI-based workflows for objective calcification assessment and to identify opportunities for investigating its potential biological and clinical relevance. Results: Current evidence indicates that calcification has been reported or proposed in vascular, stromal, necrotic, and extracellular matrix-associated contexts in OSCC and related pathological settings; however, the prevalence, biological mechanisms, and reproducibility of these patterns in OSCC remain insufficiently characterized. Potential associations with hypoxia, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, and osteogenic-like cellular reprogramming are supported primarily by evidence from broader biomineralization, vascular calcification, and other tumor contexts rather than by calcification-specific mechanistic studies in OSCC. Advances in whole-slide imaging, deep learning, and computational pathology have enabled automated tissue segmentation, feature extraction, and quantitative histopathologic analysis. However, their application to the systematic detection and spatial characterization of calcification in OSCC remains limited. AI-assisted analysis could facilitate objective identification, quantification, and spatial mapping of mineralized structures, providing a conceptual research framework for investigating tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental remodeling. title: Auditable AI agents for verifiable end-to-end scientific analysis
desc: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are evolving from research assistants into end-to-end executors, yet their capacity to generate conclusions at scale outpaces rigorous verification. Here we introduce an auditability-centred paradigm for scientific automation, wherein trust relies not on generative capability or self-evaluation, but on whether claims can be independently traced to primary evidence, reviewed and corrected. Moving beyond post-hoc checks, we embed verification throughout the research lifecycle via four principles: grounded knowledge, bounded execution, evidence-backed results and independent verification. We instantiate this paradigm in EvoTrace for viral evolutionary analysis. Distilling peer-review critiques and methodological literature, we curated 13 principles, 236 pitfalls and 50 analytical units - validating 47 across a six-tier hierarchy - to encode methodological limits as executable constraints. Across simulated benchmarks, six viral datasets and an end-to-end Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) study, claim-evidence auditing compiled evidence packages for all 233 analyses (flagging 26 incomplete evidentiary chains), while independent numerical and figure audits rectified 17 flaws, including three blocker-level errors. For CCHFV, EvoTrace intercepted a data-contradictory claim, recalibrating 'no reassortment candidates' to 'no high-confidence candidates'. By co-delivering verification evidence, auditable automation shifts AI-driven science from autonomous generation to continuous scrutiny and correction.

desc: [Frontiers in systems biology] Early detection of breast cancer is crucial for better treatment options; however, physicians usually encounter challenges when reading breast mammograms because some tissues can overlap or look similar. New computer technologies can help by highlighting areas that may contain cancer. In this study, we assessed computer systems to identify whether a breast image is normal, benign or malignant and compared their performance on standard digital mammography (DM) and digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) images. This retrospective study included 31 (100 after augmentation) images with malignant breast lesions, 175 with benign findings, and 475 normal images. We developed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) model to classify images using ResNet-18 and ResNet-50. We trained the model via 10-fold cross-validation and Holdout validation. Performance was measured for each model. We computed performance metrics on original (non-augmented) images from 10-fold cross-validated predictions, with 95% confidence intervals from a stratified patient-level bootstrap (2,000 replicates), precision-recall analysis with average precision (AP), and paired DeLong and exact McNemar tests with Holm correction. We increased the malignant class from 31 to 100 images in the training set via data augmentation for the stage-2 classifier. Validation used non-augmented images. In normal versus abnormal classification (679 original images per view; ResNet-18, 10-fold cross-validation), DM CC, DM MLO and DBT MLO achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.995 (95% CI 0.991-0.998), 0.984 (0.975-0.992) and 0.994 (0.989-0.998), sensitivity of 95.1%, 95.6% and 95.1%, and specificity of 96.6%, 94.1% and 98.5%, respectively. DBT had significantly higher specificity than DM in selected comparisons (ResNet-18 vs. DM MLO and ResNet-50 vs. DM CC; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002), with no significant AUC-ROC differences between modalities or architectures (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.13). In benign versus malignant classification (131 original images, 31 malignant), AUC-ROC ranged from 0.977 to 0.999 and AP from 0.946 to 0.996, with no significant differences between DM and DBT or between ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.50). The detection and classification of malignant, benign, and normal images in DBT and DM using an artificial intelligence (AI) training model achieved comparable performance to the medical field. title: RIPPLE: learning nucleotide relations in an RNA foundation model
desc: RNA function depends on interactions between nucleotides that can be widely separated in sequence, yet capturing these relationships remains challenging for RNA language models. Existing approaches primarily learn nucleotide relationships implicitly from individual nucleotide reconstruction or rely on external structural information to model nucleotide interactions. Here we introduce RIPPLE, an RNA foundation model that learns to identify and represent sparse, predictively useful nucleotide relationships directly from sequence. Pretrained on 32.4 million RNA sequences, RIPPLE uses pairwise predictive utility to guide relational learning, transferring training-time supervision into a sequence-only model without requiring structural inputs at inference. RIPPLE improves overall performance across five downstream tasks spanning RNA family classification, ribosome loading prediction, secondary-structure prediction, three-dimensional contact prediction, and splice-site recognition. Mechanistic analyses further show that utility-guided learning improves the recovery of informative interactions and enhances the transferability of learned RNA representations.

Artificial intelligence-guided selection of adjuvant chemotherapy and survival in gastric cancer.
source: PubMed · Gastric cancer : official journal of the International Gastric Cancer Association and the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association
desc: [Gastric cancer : official journal of the International Gastric Cancer Association and the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association] Selecting adjuvant chemotherapy for gastric cancer requires balancing tumor risk and patient-related factors. We developed and internally validated a recurrent deep survival machine (RDSM) framework to evaluate whether concordance with AI-recommended treatment is associated with overall survival (OS). This retrospective cohort study analyzed 15,848 patients with stage II-III gastric cancer from the Japanese Gastric Cancer Association (2011, 2013). Patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy, non-standard regimens, or dying within 8 weeks post-surgery were excluded. Patients were categorized as AI-recommended or AI-non-recommended based on whether their treatment matched the model-derived recommendation (the regimen with the highest predicted 5-year survival probability). Primary outcome was 5-year OS. Model performance was evaluated using the concordance index (C-index), and multiple imputation with propensity score overlap weighting (MI-OW) was used for the observational comparison of treatment concordance. RDSM showed superior discrimination compared with the Cox model (C-index, 0.77 vs. 0.73). After MI-OW, concordance with AI-recommended treatment was associated with higher 5-year OS than discordance (74.00% vs. 66.16%; adjusted difference, 7.84 percentage points [95% CI, 6.06-9.62]). A similar association was observed among patients aged ≥ 75 years (64.18% vs. 52.76%; adjusted difference, 11.42 percentage points [95% CI, 6.72-16.12]). These associations are not causal treatment effects. SHAP analyses highlighted patient-related factors for S-1 monotherapy and tumor burden for S-1 plus oxaliplatin. RDSM identified model-derived treatment patterns associated with observed OS differences, without establishing benefits from AI-guided treatment changes. External validation and prospective evaluation are needed before clinical use.

The Translation Gap in Artificial Intelligence-Based Renal Mass Characterization: A Narrative Review.
desc: [Cancers] Artificial intelligence (AI) models for solid renal mass characterization show promising discrimination in multicenter and some prospective test sets, yet little published evidence supports their routine clinical use. We examine four translation gaps. Independent, representative validation remains limited, and most studies use resected, pathologically confirmed masses, underrepresenting small indeterminate lesions managed by biopsy or surveillance. Recent multicenter models, including RenalCLIP and MPANet, broadened tasks and external testing but remain retrospective. Four retrospective reader experiments suggest that AI assistance can improve readers' accuracy or consistency, but no study identified measured effects on management or patient outcomes. Regulatory evidence is limited: one renal tool reported by its manufacturer as certified under the European Union Medical Device Regulation rests on a single-center retrospective reader study of detection and reporting, and no characterization device was identified in the U.S. Food and Drug Administration AI-enabled device list. The 2026 European Association of Urology guidelines discuss AI as an emerging technology without a graded recommendation. Cost, information technology integration, trust, and interpretability further restrict adoption. We propose a roadmap built around one intended use, the small indeterminate solid mass considered for biopsy or surveillance, with prespecified thresholds, target-specific reference standards, and paired management and safety endpoints.

Advances in Multimodal Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for the Diagnosis and Management of Diabetic Retinopathy: From Biomarkers to Personalized Care.
desc: [Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania)] Background and Objectives: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable vision loss. Staging based on colour fundus photography captures only part of a disease that involves the whole neurovascular unit and the retinal periphery. This narrative review summarizes the structural (optical coherence tomography, OCT), vascular (OCT angiography and ultra-widefield imaging) and functional (microperimetry, electrophysiology) biomarkers of DR, grades the evidence supporting each of them, and examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is changing screening, prognostication and treatment selection. Materials and Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for publications from January 2000 to May 2026, giving priority to randomized trials, prospective multicentre cohorts, systematic reviews and externally validated algorithms. Results: Among imaging biomarkers, disorganization of the retinal inner layers, outer retinal integrity and ultra-widefield angiographic non-perfusion have the most consistent prognostic evidence, whereas OCT angiography metrics remain device-dependent. AI has progressed from research classifiers to autonomous systems with regulatory authorization in the United States and the European Union, to prospectively evaluated deployments in national programmes and low-resource settings, and to time-to-event progression models and foundation models. Image-based prediction improves discrimination over clinical risk factors by modest margins, and biomarker-guided treatment of diabetic macular oedema still rests largely on retrospective series. Cross-device standardization of quantitative metrics, representative datasets, prospective outcome trials and health-economic evidence remain the main gaps. Conclusions: Individualized screening intervals are the application closest to routine practice, whereas phenotype-driven therapy and precision monitoring remain promising but unproven.

title: Artificial Intelligence across the Perioperative Continuum in Facial Plastic and Microvascular Surgery: A State-of-the-Art Narrative Review.
desc: [Facial plastic surgery : FPS] Aims and Backgrounds: Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanding applications in diagnosis, surgical planning, and postoperative care. This state-of-the-art review characterizes the growth and use of AI across perioperative care with particular attention to microvascular and free flap reconstruction, and examines how this growth compares with the pace of clinical validation. Techniques: PubMed (MEDLINE), Scopus, and Web of Science were searched through August 10, 2026 for studies evaluating AI in facial plastic surgery, oral and maxillofacial surgery, microvascular head and neck surgery, and facial reanimation. Pediatric-only, non-English, and non-AI-focused studies were excluded. Conclusions and Clinical Relevance: Of 1,249 articles, 66 met inclusion criteria. Preoperative applications accounted for 50% of studies, focusing on surgical planning, image segmentation, and risk stratification. Postoperative applications accounted for 45%, including free flap monitoring and outcome assessment. Intraoperative applications represented 6%. Deep learning and convolutional neural networks were the most common approaches, while few studies included prospective evaluation. AI use has grown rapidly in facial plastic and reconstructive surgery, with uses in preoperative planning, risk prediction, and postoperative free flap monitoring. Despite growth, clinical validation and prospective evaluation remain limited, particularly for intraoperative applications. Research focused on prospective application of technology will determine how AI can be safely incorporated into facial reconstructive surgery.

title: Comparison of Retinopathy Screening Performed Using Conventional Methods and an Artificial Intelligence-Assisted System in Prediabetic and Diabetic Patients: A Single-Center Prospective Analysis.
desc: [Medicina (Kaunas, Lithuania)] Background and Objectives: AI-assisted retinal imaging is increasingly proposed to expand diabetic retinopathy (DR) screening capacity, but most validation studies use reading-center standards, exclude prediabetes, and assess macular edema against photographic surrogates rather than optical coherence tomography (OCT). We compared an AI-assisted retinal screening system with routine ophthalmological examination in an unselected internal medicine screening population. Materials and Methods: In this prospective, cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study, consecutive adults with prediabetes or diabetes underwent AI-assisted retinal imaging (index test) followed by masked ophthalmological examination (reference standard), with OCT as the reference for macular edema. Analyses were performed at the eye level (n = 714) and patient level (n = 357) using Wilson score 95% confidence intervals and Cohen kappa (κ) for agreement. Results: Among 357 patients (714 eyes; 83.8% diabetes, 16.2% prediabetes), DR prevalence by ophthalmological examination was 15.0% (eyes) and 17.9% (patients), versus 24.4% and 33.1% by AI (McNemar p < 0.001). Eye-level and patient-level sensitivity and specificity were 70.1% and 83.7% and 75.0% and 76.1%, respectively. Negative predictive value was high (93-94%) but positive predictive value was low (41-43%); agreement was moderate at the eye level and fair at the patient level (κ = 0.428 and 0.384, respectively). False-positive AI calls were associated with higher HbA1c and albuminuria (adjusted odds ratio for log-transformed ACR 1.23, p = 0.040); false negatives had milder disease. In prediabetes, DR prevalence was 1.7% and agreement was absent (κ = -0.03). AI sensitivity for OCT-defined macular edema was 45.5% (κ = 0.197), with no significant central macular thickness difference by AI status. Conclusions: The AI system showed high negative predictive value but systematically over-called DR, with only fair-to-moderate agreement and performance below accepted screening benchmarks, particularly in prediabetes and for macular edema. These findings support its use as a rule-out triage adjunct with ophthalmological confirmation of positive results, rather than an autonomous substitute, and argue for local recalibration before deployment.

title: More than a Second Pair of Eyes: Artificial Intelligence Across the Breast Imaging Pathway.
desc: [Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland)] Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from stand-alone accuracy studies to prospective deployment across breast screening, risk prediction, multimodal diagnosis, treatment response, and workflow support. The goal of this narrative review is to determine which AI applications have demonstrated clinical benefit, which remain technically promising, and what safeguards are required for implementation. We synthesize randomized trials, prospective cohorts, real-world implementations, external validations, systematic reviews, and guidance identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus through 30 June 2026. In screening, AI-supported mammography can increase cancer detection and reduce reading workload, but effects depend on whether AI is used as concurrent support, an independent reader, triage, or partial autonomy; autonomous workflows may shift work and cost downstream through additional recalls. MASAI met its prespecified noninferiority criterion for interval cancer, but this should not be interpreted as proof of equivalence or mortality benefit. Image-based risk models often discriminate better than density or conventional clinical models, although prospective benefit from AI-guided allocation to supplemental imaging has not yet been demonstrated. Evidence for contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), MRI, ultrasound, radiomics, and multimodal models is less mature and limited by external validation, domain shift, missing data, operator dependence, and uncertain incremental value beyond clinicopathological factors. Ungrounded large language models and opaque foundation models are not suitable for autonomous clinical advice. Current evidence therefore supports controlled, task-specific integration rather than radiologist replacement; real clinical benefit depends on governance of the whole AI-enabled pathway, including local validation, human factors, downstream resource use, statistical stopping rules, and fallback procedures.

title: Artificial Intelligence for the Molecular Diagnosis of Kidney Diseases: From Computational Pathology to Noninvasive Multi-Omics.
desc: [Bioengineering (Basel, Switzerland)] Creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate and histology detect kidney disease late and say little about the molecular heterogeneity driving progression. Artificial intelligence can extract molecular features from biofluid omics; digitised biopsies and retinal images supply proxy readouts, not molecular measurements. In this review we grouped the literature by histopathology, multi-omics, foundation models and noninvasive systems and checked each result against its cohort, endpoint and validation setting. Reported performance is often high, but most results come from retrospective single-cohort evaluations; external and prospective validation are uncommon, and we found no study among those reviewed showing improved patient outcomes. High discrimination therefore establishes technical performance only; clinical utility and patient benefit remain untested. The evidence to date supports feasibility, not benefit, and the weakness lies in evaluation design rather than model architecture. The evidence so far establishes feasibility, not benefit. Until prospective studies on shared external cohorts are available, these tools are best used to augment existing diagnostic practice, with patient outcomes as the measure of success.

title: Eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases 2024 single topic symposium proceedings part 2: State of the field.
source: PubMed · Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition
desc: [Journal of pediatric gastroenterology and nutrition] While advances in the management of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) have transformed clinical practice, eosinophilic gastrointestinal diseases beyond the esophagus (non-EoE EGIDs, including eosinophilic gastritis [EoG], enteritis [EoN], and colitis [EoC]) remain incompletely defined and understudied. The 2024 North American Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition (NASPGHAN) EGID single-topic symposium (STS), EGID Xcelerating Care, Research and Innovation in an Evolving Landscape (EXCEL), Part 2-non-EoE EGIDs, highlighted emerging efforts to standardize nomenclature, diagnostic thresholds, and treatment strategies for this heterogeneous group of disorders. Histopathologic consensus criteria now distinguish disease by gastrointestinal (GI) segment, underscoring the need for site-specific biopsy sampling and recognition of additional features such as eosinophilic cryptitis, glandulitis, and submucosal involvement. Transcriptomic analyses reveal distinct molecular signatures among EoG, EoN, and EoC, suggesting variable type 2 inflammatory and non-type 2 mechanisms across the GI tract. Systemic corticosteroids are effective but limited by toxicity; dietary interventions and topical corticosteroids show inconsistent benefit; and early biologic trials targeting interleukin-4 receptor α (IL-4Rα), interleukin-5 (IL-5), and Siglec-8 demonstrate histologic improvement with variable symptom response. Advances in artificial intelligence offer promise for automating histologic assessment and integrating clinical, endoscopic, and molecular data, while health equity, patient-reported outcomes, mental health support, multidisciplinary collaboration, and seamless transition to adult care emerge as central to lifelong disease management. Through initiatives such as SPARK! (Supportive Platform for Advancing Research and Knowledge), NASPGHAN aims to accelerate discovery and mentorship in non-EoE EGIDs, catalyzing progress comparable to that achieved in EoE over the past two decades.

title: The Emerging Role and Integration of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Veterinary Education: A Narrative Review.
source: PubMed · Animals : an open access journal from MDPI
desc: [Animals : an open access journal from MDPI] Artificial intelligence (AI), a data-driven and algorithm-supported technological system, has rapidly expanded its role in transforming daily life and professional practice over the past decade. In this narrative review, the recent literature was examined to evaluate current and emerging applications of AI in veterinary education and practice. A previously reported PubMed-focused search and a broader literature compilation served different purposes. The historical screening counts cannot be fully reconstructed, and the synthesis was narrative rather than systematic. Veterinary schools in the United States and elsewhere have begun exploring and integrating AI into Doctor of Veterinary Medicine (DVM) curricula to support teaching, learning, and competency development. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI in veterinary education. In anatomy, AI-based visualization and interactive tools are being explored, although controlled evidence of improved learning outcomes remains limited. In digital pathology, AI-assisted image analysis can provide students with opportunities to develop skills in recognizing and interpreting pathological findings. In clinical settings, AI models have shown potential in selected imaging and clinical-classification tasks, but their educational effectiveness requires further evaluation. Despite these advances, the broader implementation of AI in veterinary education and practice faces important regulatory and ethical challenges, including concerns regarding data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-generated information. Addressing these issues will require multidisciplinary collaboration, multicenter data integration, appropriate validation, and strong ethical governance. With these foundations in place, AI may serve as a supportive educational and clinical tool rather than a replacement for veterinary educators and professionals. In the future, appropriately validated AI tools may contribute to veterinary education and clinical training.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Endodontics: A Narrative Review and Critical Synthesis of Diagnostic, Predictive, and Operational Applications.
desc: [Dentistry journal] Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) research in endodontics has grown quickly, but the strength of the evidence differs between applications. This narrative review with structured evidence mapping examined diagnostic imaging, canal morphology, outcome prediction, large language models (LLMs), robotics and augmented reality, and operational uses such as case-difficulty assessment, triage and scheduling. Methods: Two anchor reviews were combined with a documented PubMed search to 30 September 2026, and studies were classified by design, sample, reference standard, validation, and evidence of clinical utility. Results: Periapical lesion detection has the largest evidence base: one meta-analysis reported pooled sensitivity of 0.925 and specificity of 0.852, although most included studies were at risk of bias and none was prospective. Fracture detection relies mainly on ex vivo data and is sensitive to image resolution. Outcome models showed modest to moderate discrimination in single-centre data. LLM studies reported 40% to 100% correct, appropriate, or concordant responses across different benchmarks and scoring rules, and outputs varied on repeated querying. Difficulty-assessment and scheduling tools have appeared since 2020 but have not been evaluated prospectively in clinical workflow. Conclusions: Technical performance has not yet been shown to translate into clinical benefit, and AI in endodontics should currently be used only as clinician-supervised decision support.

title: From innovation to implementation: perspectives from Chief Health AI Officers.
desc: [npj health systems] Drawing on perspectives from interviews with four pioneering chief health artificial intelligence officers (CHAIOs), this editorial examines how executive AI leadership transforms health systems. Insights reveal CHAIOs combine technical fluency in AI with clinical and operational expertise to drive impact. As the use of health AI expands, interviewees emphasize that specialized leadership is not only essential for effective AI governance but also critical for its safe and sustainable use.

title: Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence for Biomedical Applications-3rd Edition.
desc: [Bioengineering (Basel, Switzerland)] The integration of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) into biomedicine has rapidly evolved from proof-of-concept algorithmic experimentation to fully operational decision-support frameworks and precision-medicine applications [...].

title: From Generative Biology to Evidence-Centric Drug Discovery.
desc: [Pharmaceuticals (Basel, Switzerland)] Generative and predictive artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing the number of molecular, structural, cellular, and therapeutic hypotheses that can be explored computationally. Experimental capacity, however, has not expanded at a comparable rate. The result is an evidence bottleneck, in which biological hypotheses are generated faster than they can be experimentally tested, reproduced, and translated. This mismatch is particularly consequential for pharmaceutical discovery, where computational predictions alone cannot establish biological function, mechanism, or therapeutic value. As the number of computationally generated hypotheses grows, the central challenge shifts from candidate generation to the prioritization of hypotheses for experimental validation. This evidence bottleneck represents a defining constraint of AI-enabled biological discovery. We examine how different biological claims, including structural, interaction, functional, mechanistic, and therapeutic claims, require distinct types and levels of evidence. We also address the cost and context-dependence of experimental validation. Furthermore, we discuss how information-guided experimental design and iterative model-experiment feedback can improve the allocation of limited experimental capacity. We propose an evidence-centric framework for drug discovery that extends the evaluation of generative models beyond their ability to generate or rank hypotheses. The framework emphasizes experimental testability, mechanistic understanding, reproducibility, and translation into actionable biological and therapeutic knowledge.

title: Death, Existentialism, and the Personalised Patient Preference Predictor.
desc: [Bioethics] It has recently been proposed that fine-tuned large-language models (LLMs) could more accurately predict the preferences of incapacitated patients than surrogates. This hypothetical technology has been named the personalised patient preference predictor (P4). Advocates of the P4 claim that the P4 will not only more accurately predict patient preferences, but will better respect patient autonomy, facilitate the composition of advance directives, and reduce the emotional burden of surrogate decision-making. I challenge these purported benefits by arguing that the P4 would pose a substantive risk to our ability to meaningfully grapple with death. Drawing on the philosophies of Søren Kierkegaard and Martin Heidegger, I argue that adopting an existential attitude towards death is central to the pursuit of an ethical life. Implementation of the P4 risks inhibiting both patients and surrogates from adopting an existential attitude towards death, with deleterious consequences.

title: Dual-Model Collaboration with Consistency Calibration for Intelligent Acupuncture Prescription Recommendation.
source: PubMed · Chinese journal of integrative medicine
desc: [Chinese journal of integrative medicine] A dual-model collaborative framework for intelligent acupuncture prescription recommendation was proposed. Specifically, symptom-to-acupoint mapping was formulated as an end-to-end text generation task and an intelligent recommendation method based on dual-model collaboration with consistency calibration (DM3C) was proposed. By combining a domain-fine-tuned generator, retrieval-augmented LLM outputs, and a consistency-calibrated random forest filter, the proposed DM3C enhances the generalizability and recall of intelligent acupuncture prescription recommendations, these findings demonstrate its potential as an auxiliary acupoint recommendation tool.

title: AI-FPGA Integration in Nanosatellite and Small-Satellite Systems: An Evidence-Stratified Systematic Mapping Review.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] This evidence-stratified systematic mapping review evaluates artificial intelligence (AI) and field-programmable gate array (FPGA) technologies in nanosatellite and small-satellite systems. A preserved Scopus screening history retained 67 records published from 2015 to 8 September 2026; deduplication left 65 unique records, comprising 56 primary studies and nine contextual sources. A subsequent eligibility audit identified four primary records unsuitable for strict satellite-specific inference, yielding 52 analytically eligible primary studies without altering historical screening counts. Earth observation represented 30 of the original 56 primary records. A source-traced technical audit distinguishes directly verified values, absent metrics in examined full texts, and source-limited fields. Detailed primary-source verification confirms in-orbit OPS-SAT inference on Cyclone V at 24-25 microseconds per patch and 1.4-1.5 W average power. It also reclassifies a fuzzy attitude controller study as behavioral simulation and separates Versal AI Engine execution from programmable logic resources. Heterogeneous data, devices, baselines, and validation conditions prevent pooled performance rankings across computing architectures. The contribution is an auditable mission-model-hardware and validation maturity map, together with explicit limitations on technical and flight heritage evidence.

title: Marine particles as underexplored hotspots for antimicrobial peptide discovery: an ecology-guided frontier in marine natural product bioprospecting.
desc: [Frontiers in microbiology] The increasing global antibiotic resistance has created a pressing need for new antimicrobial drugs. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) come into the spotlight for their antibacterial properties, particularly against multidrug-resistant pathogens. Because AMPs typically mediate localized interference competition, we hypothesize that spatially confined, highly competitive microbiomes create ecological conditions that favor the evolution, expression, and diversification of AMPs, although spatial structure may equally promote niche partitioning, cooperative interactions, and producer-resistant coexistence. We therefore propose, as a working hypothesis, that marine particles represent promising yet underexplored reservoirs of untapped marine AMPs. Marine particles are ubiquitous throughout the ocean, ranging from the sunlit surface waters to the deepest hadal environments. They are densely colonized microhabitats where nutrient gradients, spatial proximity, chemical signaling, and interspecies competition among microorganisms converge-unique characteristics that position marine particles as natural laboratories for the evolution of novel AMPs. However, most marine microorganisms are challenging to cultivate. Fortunately, metagenomics is greatly expanding the scope of marine AMP discovery by enabling researchers to screen for elusive peptide-encoding genes and complex biosynthetic gene clusters in uncultivated microbial communities. Additionally, advancements in artificial intelligence are further transforming marine AMP bioprospecting by moving from passive exploration to active molecular understanding and navigation. This review synthesizes our current understanding of the microbial ecology and emerging technologies that drive marine AMP discovery, and explores the application potentials of marine AMPs in human medicine, agriculture, and mariculture.

title: POSNNET: Positioning Neural Network Estimation Tool.
desc: [Sensors (Basel, Switzerland)] Many applications rely on IMU and GNSS data for localization, typically fused using algorithms such as the Kalman filter or its variants. Although this approach provides accurate localization without requiring additional infrastructure, its performance degrades in GNSS-denied environments. Deep learning methods have been proposed to address this issue in real time; however, because they do not leverage future data, they yield suboptimal reconstructions in applications that do not require real-time processing. To overcome this limitation, we introduce POSNNET, a post-processing framework designed to reconstruct position and velocity during prolonged periods of weak or absent GNSS signals. POSNNET is intended for localization scenarios in which real-time processing is not required, including sports performance analysis, infrastructure-free road mapping, and wildlife tracking, although its applicability across these domains requires further validation. The framework estimates velocity using state-of-the-art neural networks that leverage both past and future IMU and GNSS data. Position is subsequently recovered through weighted bidirectional integration. To improve reconstruction accuracy and consistency, the outputs of multiple neural networks are combined. POSNNET was validated offline against causal real-time baselines using simulated GNSS outages in a 100-h outdoor equestrian dataset characterized by higher speeds and more complex dynamics than typical pedestrian motion, with the sensor-fusion output serving as the reference trajectory. It achieved average trajectory errors, relative to this reference, of 4.07 m for simulated GNSS outages lasting from 30 s to 2 min and 7.06 m for outages lasting from 2 to 5 min, corresponding to an 93.4% (for outages lasting 30 s to 2 min) and 95.6% (for outages lasting 2 to 5 min) improvement in accuracy over the strongest evaluated real-time state-of-the-art method.

title: AI Identity Threat and Job Crafting Among University Teachers.
desc: [Behavioral sciences (Basel, Switzerland)] Generative artificial intelligence can challenge teachers' professional self-evaluations, yet how these concerns relate to subsequent work behavior remains unclear. We examined AI identity threat, supervisor-directed feedback seeking, and individual job crafting in a three-wave study at two universities in central China (n = 563 at baseline). The behavioral measures were adapted to an AI-related work context. A multiple-indicator random-intercept cross-lagged panel model separated stable differences between teachers from fluctuations within teachers. Higher-than-usual threat was associated with greater subsequent feedback seeking in both intervals (β = 0.428 and 0.398). Feedback seeking was associated with subsequent job crafting in the second interval (β = 0.553), whereas evidence in the first interval was inconclusive (β = 0.194, p = 0.130). The specific T1 threat-T2 feedback seeking-T3 crafting sequence showed a positive prospective indirect association (b = 0.266; 95% Monte Carlo CI [0.112, 0.459]). The feedback-to-crafting coefficients differed statistically, but unequal observation intervals and possible academic-calendar influences limit interpretation of this difference. The findings suggest that teachers' requests for supervisory feedback may connect AI-related identity concerns with later work adjustment.

title: The Werther effect: media influence, psychosocial mechanisms, and suicide prevention (a narrative review).
desc: [Frontiers in psychiatry] Suicide-related media communication may contribute to both harmful and protective outcomes, depending on the characteristics of the content, individual vulnerability, and the broader communication context. The Werther effect describes increased suicidal behavior associated with certain forms of suicide-related media exposure, whereas the Papageno effect refers to potentially protective responses to narratives emphasizing coping, recovery, and alternatives to suicide. This narrative review critically synthesizes evidence concerning these contrasting effects, their proposed psychosocial mechanisms, and their implications for contemporary suicide prevention. Literature searches were conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection, initially in July 2026 and subsequently updated in October 2026. Relevant historical publications and recent studies addressing digital communication, algorithmic exposure, and artificial intelligence were also considered. Evidence from traditional media research supports associations between particular reporting practices and subsequent suicide mortality, especially following highly publicized celebrity suicides. In contrast, experimental studies of recovery-oriented communication suggest favorable short-term psychological responses, although evidence of sustained behavioral benefits remains limited. Emerging research highlights the complexity of digital suicide-related communication, including algorithmically mediated exposure, real-time audience interactions, and the potential role of emotional contagion, although their specific contributions to suicidal outcomes remain uncertain. The clinical effectiveness and safety of artificial intelligence-based suicide prevention applications also remain insufficiently established. Interpretation of these findings is complicated by methodological heterogeneity, potential confounding, and differences in measured outcomes. Overall, responsible suicide communication should be integrated into comprehensive prevention strategies, with greater emphasis on evaluating clinically meaningful outcomes and distinguishing harmful exposure from protective communication.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Dentistry and Orofacial Sciences: From Promising Algorithms to Trustworthy Clinical Decisions.
desc: [Bioengineering (Basel, Switzerland)] A few years ago, artificial intelligence (AI) in dentistry was mostly a topic for conference keynotes and proof-of-concept papers [...].

title: Computational Neuroscience and Artificial Intelligence: Cross-Talks and Interrelated Contributions.
desc: [Brain sciences] The convergence of computational neuroscience and artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming how we understand neural information processing and develop technologies inspired by, and interacting with, the nervous system [...].
